cards.label: C015
cards.hyp: Meter on GPIO39 (L RPWM) with RST held reads ≈ 3.3 V (ESP32-S3 boot pull-up); with 10 kΩ from GPIO39 to GND it reads < 0.8 V. GPIO40–42 read < 0.8 V in normal boot.
cards.note: Found in the T3 review. Do it BEFORE the first bts7960 bench run. DevKit on USB only, BTS7960 not connected. Meter DC V, GPIO39 → GND: (1) sketch running, (2) RST held, (3) BUT1 + RST held (download mode). Repeat for GPIO40, 41, 42. Then 10 kΩ GPIO39 → GND and repeat (2). Until this is closed: rocker in KILL whenever you flash or press reset, RUN only after the banner. The result decides 10 kΩ pull-downs on GPIO39–42 in pcb/carrier-revA/SPEC.md and on breadboards 1/2b (firmware/armini uses the same pins). Source: github.com/mcuw/esp32-s3-pinouts. Photo: meter display at each step, C015_NN.
cards.result: STEP D 11.10 ~18:50. DevKit on USB only, `ladder` sketch, which does not touch 39–42. Meter DC V to EXT2 pin 1 GND. Readings (1) sketch running / (2) EN held low (reset) / (3) download mode (GPIO0 low + RST): GPIO39 (EXT2-9, L RPWM) 3.148 / 0.020 / 3.231 · GPIO40 (EXT2-8, L LPWM) 0.022 / 0.020 / 3.236 · GPIO41 (EXT2-7, R RPWM) 0.020 / 0.018 / 0.023 · GPIO42 (EXT2-6, R LPWM) 0.022 / 0.021 / 0.025. 10 kΩ GPIO39→GND in reset: 0, but that says nothing because 39 is already 0 in reset. HYPOTHESIS PARTLY WRONG: in reset all four pins are LOW. The danger is AFTER reset. (a) GPIO39 stays HIGH when the code does not drive it, so from reset until setup() drives it LOW the left BTS7960 sees RPWM = 1, LPWM = 0, which is FULL FORWARD if its EN pins are high. (b) In download mode (flashing) 39 AND 40 are HIGH: both half-bridges high = brake, but the order in which they rise is unknown. Right driver (41/42) stays LOW in all three states. NEXT (5 min): 10 kΩ GPIO39→GND in state 1 and state 3, and 10 kΩ GPIO40→GND in state 3. If it drops < 0.8 V, it is a weak pull-up and 10 k pull-downs fix it. If it stays ~3 V, the pin is DRIVEN, and only gating the BTS EN pins (low at boot) or moving the PWM pins fixes it. Until closed: rocker in KILL when flashing or resetting. 10 kΩ REDO 19:06: GPIO39 in state 1, GPIO39 in state 3 and GPIO40 in state 3 all read ~0 V. So the HIGH is very weak, and a 10 kΩ pull-down overrides it completely. A typical ~45 kΩ internal pull-up would still leave ~0.6 V, so the pins may simply be floating; a pull-down fixes both cases. DECISION (Teddy + Claude 11.10): 10 kΩ pull-downs to GND on GPIO39, 40, 41 and 42 on the breadboard now, on the perfboard (C031) and on carrier rev B (C032). Firmware drives the four pins LOW first thing in setup(). The rocker stays the hardware layer: R_EN/L_EN go through its RUN pole, so KILL cuts both drivers whatever the PWM pins do. SANITY CHECK 19:15: resistor out → 3.2 V, resistor in → 0, so the zeros are real. CLOSED 11.10 19:15 · Partial: the hypothesis was right about the 10 kΩ and about 40–42 in normal boot, but wrong about reset (all LOW in reset; the HIGH comes after it and in download mode). Written into hardware/wiring/PINOUT.md item 4, pins_devkit.h and STATE.md (for Cursor to commit). Was: (1) 1-min sanity check: resistor out in state 1 → ~3.1 V again, resistor in → ~0; (2) optional logic-analyzer capture of 39–42 through 3 × RST and one flash with the 4 pull-downs fitted, no BTS7960 connected, all lines LOW except when the sketch drives them (catches short pulses a meter misses).

This card = the prototype fix by hand in the two black PLA brackets from C037. The CAD fix (cable slot in pivot_bracket and in the cam pan block + a FAILS line) is a separate Cursor job.

1) MEASURE, servo out, caliper on the outlet: a = width across the 20 mm side of the body; b = how far it sticks out of the end; c = ear underside → outlet top; d = ear underside → outlet bottom. Photo estimate: c ≈ 8–9, d ≈ 16 mm.

2) MARK with a pencil. Where: the END WALL of the pocket at the end nearer the idler pin (= where the spline goes; same rule on the mirrored bracket). Centre: halfway between the two insert holes of that end. Width: a + 1 mm. Depth: from the top face down to d + 1 mm (≈ 17). Through the whole end wall (~9 mm) to the outside, so the wire leaves sideways and nothing gets pinched under the ear.

3) CUT (Dremel 4000 is on the bench since 13.10 evening, BOM 136–138): bracket in the Multi-Vise 2500 by the servo block, soft jaws or a rag, never clamped on the idler pin. Thin cut-off wheel on the flex shaft, LOW speed (dial 10–15 k, PLA melts above that): two vertical cuts on the marks, stop 1 mm short of the depth line, break the tab out with the flush cutters, finish the bottom with a sanding drum or a file. Glasses on, the wheel throws PLA chips. Without the Dremel: junior hacksaw or a craft knife in several passes. No hot soldering tip for cutting: it smears, fumes, and softens the insert holes next to it.

4) INSERT HOLES at that end: they are 9.65 apart (d4), so only ~5.6 mm of plastic between them. A slot wider than ~5 mm opens them: fine, no inserts at that end. The servo is then held by the snug pocket + the 2 inserts at the far end, enough for C019 (unpowered, swung by hand).

5) DRY FIT: servo in by hand with the outlet in the slot. Pass if the ears lie flat on the block face (no gap you can see from the side) and the wire comes out of the slot freely. If it still stops: the slot is not deep enough, take 1 mm more off the bottom. Then the second bracket the same way.

6) Only after both fit: inserts (ruthex M3, HS-03 ~220 °C). Then C019 goes on from step 4.

Photos: the pencil marks, the cut slot from above, the servo seated (side view, ears on the face). Write a b c d in the result.

The servo now seats with its ears on the block face (C019_04) and arm_drive is on the disc horn (C019_07). Edges of the hole are torn PLA: round them with the knife or a sanding drum so the cable insulation is not cut. a b c d were not measured (eyeballed hole). Note for next time: the bracket was held by hand on the drill base (C019_06, video): clamp it in the base slots or the Multi-Vise. The hole most likely clipped the two insert holes at that end: no inserts there, 2 screws at the far end + the pocket hold the servo (as planned). Second bracket: same hole.

cards.hyp: With both thermal cameras on one MG90S on the arch, a closed loop (hot-spot column → pan angle) keeps a 37 °C target within ±1 thermal pixel (~3.4° on the 110° camera) of the image centre while the robot turns at its normal rate, and sweeps ±80° (~270° coverage with the 110° FOV) in < 1 s per side.
cards.note: AFTER G1 (for G2, 30.12.2026). Decision 23.10: v1 cameras FIXED on the arch (forward, 15° down), the robot turns on its tracks/thrusters to look sideways. Why pan later: (1) wider view without turning the boat, turning in water is slow and drifts; (2) target tracking = a closed loop camera → angle → servo, strong for the portfolio; (3) aim the narrow camera where the wide one saw a hot spot. Cost: angle calibration, cable flex at every turn (5 cm slack loop, limit ±80°), one more failure point. Design rule NOW: the fixed v1 mount must take the same camera plate as the pan version, so the plate can move onto an MG90S without reprinting the tube clamp. Servo: MG90S (chosen 20.10; TD-8120MGs are in the pivot brackets, ST3215 too big for the pocket). Both thermal boards on ONE servo, not one servo each. OV3660 stays fixed on the XIAO. Before starting: measure the MG90S (body 22.4 × 12, ear plane 16, ear holes 27.7 from the catalogue) and its horn; PCA9685 channel to be assigned.

ORDER: (1) M4 depth: screw one stock M4 (28.4 long) into a thruster insert by hand and count turns / measure how far it goes; if it bottoms before ~10 mm the insert is blind → M4 × 12 from the DSM set (plate 5 + frame ~9.7). Never force a long screw into a blind insert: it cracks the thruster boss. (2) Thruster on the arm: 4 × M4 through the 50 × 30 plate, cross pattern, hand-tight. (3) Hinge: push the Ø5 rod (60 mm, 5 mm aluminium) through lug – cheek – cheek – lug. It must turn freely; if the 5.3 holes are tight, ream by twisting the rod with a drop of water, or run the 5 mm bit through each hole. R-clip (or a 2 mm pin) at both ends. (4) Lock pin: M3 × 20 (or the 3 mm rod) through lug + cheek at r 10 in the deployed hole (−32°); the stowed hole is +68°. Check both. (5) Bracket on the hull: 4 × ruthex M3 into the transom pad's blind holes (HS-03 at 220 °C, chamfer first, flush), then 4 × M3 × 10 through the 6.2 × 3 counterbores. The bracket plate must sit flat on the pad; if it rocks, find the high spot (brim remnant / elephant foot) and scrape. (6) Swing test by hand: deployed against the stop, kick up to +100°, back down; the duct must clear the hull bottom and the transom at every angle. Then the same on the other hull. analyses.challenge: The boat's whole premise is finding a person in water with a low-cost thermal array (MLX90640 / 90642). Testing it needs a repeatable target: a 1:9 figure that floats head-out, stays near 37 °C at the head for 20+ minutes in cold water, survives the lift, and is cheap to rebuild. Scaling is the catch — a 1:9 head has 1/81 of the area, so at 1 m the camera sees a few warm pixels, not a face.
analyses.decision: Warm pack now (the v1 video) and a measured bench test (C029: Pesho at 37 °C from 1 m) with the angular size written down. For the real-water phase add a full-size warm target, so the detection numbers mean something at 1:1.

impact.note: Drowning is a leading cause of accidental death; a cheap detector that works at night is direct nature & people impact. Financial: a real product niche. Scientific: new numbers for low-cost arrays.

analyses.lesson: A scaled demonstrator scales geometry, not physics: thermal contrast, pixel size and water cooling do not scale with the hull. Say which numbers are 1:9 and which are 1:1.

options.what: Hot-water bottle / warm gel pack inside the head — cheap, 10–15 min of useful contrast, no electronics
Resistive heater + thermistor + a small controller at 37 °C — stable for hours, needs a battery and a seal
Phase-change hand warmer (sodium acetate) — a flat plateau near 50 °C: too hot for a 'human', but a clean, repeatable source
